title: Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act
official_title: To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to exclude from gross income any damages, other than punitive damages, received on account of any sexual acts or sexual contact.
likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Republican in the Republican-majority House, and the bill carries 3 cosponsors. The exclusion for non-punitive damages received on account of sexual acts or contact has cross-ideological appeal that limits opposition, though Senate passage would require 60 votes.
summary: This bill lets people exclude from their taxable income money awarded for sexual acts or sexual contact, other than punitive damages, whether or not there are medical records or visible injuries. It also makes a written statement in a court decision or settlement enough to shift the burden of proof to the IRS and directs Treasury to publicize the tax break.
brief: Excludes non-punitive damages received on account of sexual acts or sexual contact from federal taxable income.

top_lines.headline: Tax Exclusion for Abuse Damages
subs: Excludes non-punitive damages for sexual acts or sexual contact from gross income
Applies whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries

top_lines.headline: Burden of Proof Shift
subs: A decision or agreement stating damages are for sexual acts counts as credible evidence
Treats the taxpayer as meeting the burden-of-proof requirements of Section 7491(a)

top_lines.headline: Public Awareness Program
subs: Treasury must run a program to publicize the exclusion
Coordinated with the Justice Department's Office on Violence Against Women

items.main: Amends Section 104(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code to exclude from gross income damages received on account of a sexual act or sexual contact.
items.detail: The exclusion covers damages other than punitive damages and applies whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries. 'Sexual act' and 'sexual contact' are defined by reference to Section 2246 of Title 18, United States Code, as in effect on enactment.

items.main: Provides that a decision or agreement stating that damages are on account of a sexual act or sexual contact is treated as credible evidence of that fact.
items.detail: For purposes of Section 7491(a), such a statement is treated as credible evidence and the taxpayer is treated as having met the requirements of Section 7491(a)(2) on whether the damages are on account of the act or contact.

sections.label: Section 2(d)-(e) - No Inference and Public Awareness

items.main: Bars drawing inferences about the physical-injury exclusion and directs Treasury to promote public awareness of the new exclusion.
items.detail: No inference may be drawn from the amendment about whether 'personal physical injuries or physical sickness' includes injuries without medical records or observable injuries. The Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Justice Department's Office on Violence Against Women, must conduct a program to promote public awareness of the exclusion.

underreported.summary: Treats a decision or agreement's statement that damages are on account of a sexual act or contact as credible evidence and deems the taxpayer to have met the Section 7491(a)(2) burden-of-proof requirements.
underreported.why_unreported: Beyond creating a tax exclusion, this changes the evidentiary burden in tax disputes over whether damages qualify, an effect not signaled by the exclusion itself.

gaps: The bill applies the exclusion only to decisions made and agreements entered after enactment and does not address claims or agreements predating enactment.
The bill treats a decision or agreement's characterization as credible evidence but does not address damages where the decision or agreement does not state their basis.
The bill directs Treasury to run a public-awareness program but sets no timeline or funding for it.
The bill excludes non-punitive damages for sexual acts or contact but does not specify how awards covering both sexual and non-sexual claims are allocated.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smith
featured_quotes.text: Survivors of sexual assault face a long road to recovery without having to battle with the IRS over keeping the compensatory damages or settlements that they receive. Unfortunately, right now, the burden of proof that a sexual assault survivor would have to provide to the IRS, including medical records to prove that they deserve to have their settlement funds excluded from gross income for tax purposes, ignores the fact that such victims often do not have the same observable physical injuries that other victims of assault might have.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smucker
featured_quotes.text: I think the chairman and Ms. Moore both have described it really well. The core problem here, first of all, we believe our current law already says that any victim of physical abuse and any victim of sexual abuse who receives a settlement does not owe tax on that settlement, which makes complete sense.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Moore
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, we hear all the time about the high-profile civil cases involving sexual abuse. I am thinking about the accounts of trusted gymnast physicians abusing star athletes and the victims of Jeffrey Epstein and many of his associates. We even hear about sexual assault that occurs within our own body, and we have to address that problem. Let's just take a moment to acknowledge that all sexual abuse does not make the headlines.

added: An income-tax exclusion for non-punitive damages received on account of a sexual act or sexual contact
A burden-of-proof rule treating a decision or agreement's characterization as credible evidence under Section 7491(a)
A Treasury public-awareness program conducted with the Justice Department's Office on Violence Against Women
modified: Section 104(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code amended to exclude damages for sexual acts or contact, whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries
